accuracy.evidence: Checked against Chin, Tokaryk, Erickson and Calk (1998) Nature 393: 680-682: the Saskatchewan specimen (Frenchman Formation, Maastrichtian) is about 44 cm long, 30-50% bone fragments of juvenile primary bone from a young plant-eating (ornithischian) dinosaur, and attributed to a tyrannosaur, 'most likely Tyrannosaurus rex', from its size, contents and time and place; the Royal Saskatchewan Museum release names a juvenile duck-billed or horned dinosaur as the prey. Coprolite naming by Buckland (1829) after Mary Anning's observation of fish bones and scales in 'bezoar stones' from Lyme Regis ichthyosaurs, and the Greek roots, checked against the Natural History Museum and Lyme Regis Museum accounts. Rapid burial and mineral replacement, phosphate favouring carnivore coprolites, and thin sections and CT scans as methods match Chin's papers. Chin (2007) Palaios: rotted conifer wood in coprolites attributed to hadrosaurs. Triceratops, a tyrannosaur and small dromaeosaurs are all known from the Frenchman Formation. Every parameterised item checked at its range corners (10+2 to 40+9, 2+1 to 6+5, 35-30 to 44-30, 3+2 to 9+6).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented naive ideas: a coprolite is still soft, smelly poo (prediction, challenge 'soft'), any dropping left out becomes a fossil (the 'dries in the sun' card is refused with why burial must be fast), big dung means a big plant-eater (Triceratops refused for the bone-filled coprolite; bone poo sorted to plant-eater refused), and the maker is known for certain (the 'T. rex, for sure' card is refused as too sure; prediction 'Yes, always'), plus the opposite slip that it is 'just a rock that tells us nothing'.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagdung works on coprolites themselves: ordering burial and mineralisation, a drag-to-cut action that opens a lump into a cross-section showing bone with pores, a seed, striped wood and a ringed fish scale to be named, diet sorting from contents, a ruler with a draggable arrow to measure the 44 cm specimen before picking from the three dinosaurs of the Frenchman Formation, and a We can say / Too sure claim sort. It is not 543 flagfoss (body-fossil formation), 893 flagfossev (fossils as evidence of change), 1018 flagtrack (trackways) or 559 flagdino; the 6-token shingle gate reports no flag lab above 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is found by doing: the sun card bounces, so burial is needed; cutting reveals what is inside, so slices are how scientists look; bone sorted to plant-eater is refused, so contents give diet; measuring 44 cm and then trying Triceratops or the small raptor shows size and contents together point to a big meat-eater; 'T. rex, for sure' bounces from We can say, so the learner meets 'most likely'. Each DONE line then states the rule.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'Yes, it is still poo' (the steps end in stone), 'A plant-eater' for a bone-filled coprolite (refused in the diet sort), and 'Yes, always' for being sure of the maker (the 'for sure' claim is refused as too sure). The reveal line names the right answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven questions, each wrong option tied to a named slip: soft poo, egg, fish versus plants, big plant-eater, small raptor size, smelling or melting instead of slicing or scanning, drying in the sun, being sure, and 'nothing: just a rock'. Clicked through with chal.cjs.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and concrete words (poo, mud, stone, bone, seeds), with coprolite and minerals explained at first use; adult text gives the history, method and the 1998 study in plain language; both are within the validator limits. Canvas text is a short heading per scene, short cards and a ruler with numbers every 10 cm.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs: what a coprolite is and how it forms; how scientists look inside and what the bits mean; the 44 cm Canadian coprolite; why it is a best guess. Adult paragraphs: history and curriculum fit; formation, methods and the two studies; named common mistakes; what the lab does. The content gate finds no filler phrase.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px phone screenshots in light and dark for all five scenes: the five step cards in a 2-column grid with four numbered slots below, the cut line drawn while dragging and the slice filling most of the width with the four bits spaced apart and labels below, five coprolite cards with a small lump icon and contents text, the ruler across the full width with an arrow handle large enough to drag and +/-1 and +/-5 cm buttons, and claim cards in a 2-column grid above the two bins.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: 'Next: Mud covers it fast' style step buttons, 'Cut a slice', a naming button per bit described by shape ('Bit with tiny holes', 'Round bit with a line'), 'bone → Meat-eater' diet buttons, ruler buttons announcing the arrow position, maker buttons, and 'Can say' / 'Too sure' per claim. The canvas aria-label carries each scene description and every piece of feedback including the ruler reading; challenge feedback is a role=status live region; ✓ and ✗ mark state as well as colour; axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes.
